# Stress fractures

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > Lower extremity > Stress fractures*

[Original Article Link](/library/2F0Th3)

---

## Summary

A <u>stress</u> <u>fracture</u> is a <u>fracture</u> of structurally normal bone due to the coalescence of microfractures caused by repetitive activity. <u>Risk factors</u> include female sex, <u>calcium</u> deficiency, and highly repetitive activity. Clinical manifestations include <u>pain</u> that worsens with activity and improves with rest and tenderness over the affected bone. <u>High-risk stress fractures</u> are <u>stress</u> <u>fractures</u> in locations (e.g., <u>lateral</u> femoral neck, <u>anterior</u> <u>tibia</u>, 5<sup>th</sup> <u>metatarsal</u>) that are <u>prone</u> to complications (e.g., <u>fracture</u> progression, <u>nonunion</u>). <u>Stress</u> <u>fractures</u> may be managed based on a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>, but <u>x-rays</u> are typically obtained for confirmation. Because <u>x-rays</u> are often normal, an <u>MRI</u> is indicated if there is a concern for a <u>high-risk stress fracture</u>. Treatment is mainly conservative and focuses on cessation of the inciting activity, but <u>high-risk stress fractures</u> are managed as acute <u>fractures</u>, with <u>immobilization</u>, avoidance of <u>weight-bearing</u> activities, and referral to orthopedics.

---

## Etiology

### Mechanism




Normal bone develops a <u>fracture</u> as a result of <u>bone remodeling</u> due to repetitive microtrauma.  [[5]](/library/uy1pSj0)[[6]](/library/bB1HzQ0)




### <u>Risk factors</u> [[6]](/library/bB1HzQ0)[[7]](/library/cy1aVj0)




* Participation in repetitive high-intensity physical activity: often seen in athletes and military recruits, and children and <u>adolescents</u> participating in year-round sports  [[3]](/library/s3WtPO0)[[8]](/library/ZRWZlO0)

* Improper technique during physical activity

* Ill-fitting footwear

* Poor nutrition and/or low calorie intake (e.g., in <u>anorexia nervosa</u>)

* Low <u>bone mineral density</u>

* <u>Calcium</u> and/or <u>vitamin D deficiency</u>

* Female sex   [[9]](/library/A0WRiP0)

* Previous <u>stress</u> <u>fracture</u> [[2]](/library/Uy1bej0)





> [!TIP]
> The <u>female athlete triad syndrome</u> is associated with an increased risk of <u>stress</u> <u>fractures</u>. [[2]](/library/Uy1bej0)

---

## Clinical features

* Location [[10]](/library/zr1rPR0)

* Lower extremities (most common): <u>tibia</u>, tarsal <u>navicular</u>, <u>metatarsals</u> (<u>march fracture</u>), <u>femur</u>, <u>fibula</u>, <u>pelvis</u>

* Upper extremities (least common): <u>humerus</u>, <u>scapula</u>, <u>ribs</u>

* Symptoms [[6]](/library/bB1HzQ0)[[7]](/library/cy1aVj0)

* <u>Pain</u> that worsens with activity and resolves with rest  

* Typically begins several weeks after an increase in exercise intensity

* Usually well localized

* <u>Fractures</u> may be asymptomatic (incidental finding). [[11]](/library/2y1Tej0)

* Signs [[2]](/library/Uy1bej0)[[7]](/library/cy1aVj0)

* Focal bone tenderness, <u>erythema</u>, and/or <u>soft tissue</u> swelling

* Provocation test reproduces <u>pain</u>

* Rotation of the hip exacerbates <u>pain</u> from a <u>proximal</u> <u>femur</u> <u>stress</u> <u>fracture</u>.

* <u>Hop test</u> exacerbates <u>pain</u> from a lower extremity <u>stress</u> <u>fracture</u>.

* <u>Foot inversion</u> exacerbates <u>pain</u> in <u>metatarsal stress fracture</u>.





![Metatarsal stress fractures](media/c8titlggd5s396te8r7lg8n0.jpg)

Metatarsal stress fractures

---

## Diagnosis

### Imaging




A preliminary <u>clinical diagnosis</u> guides early management, but imaging of the affected region is indicated for confirmation. [[2]](/library/Uy1bej0)[[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* <u>X-ray</u>: recommended initial imaging study [[5]](/library/uy1pSj0)

* Radiographic features of stress fractures include: [[7]](/library/cy1aVj0)

* <u>Fracture</u> line: line of faint lucency

* Indirect features: periosteal thickening, increased cortical density, formation of a <u>callus</u>, endosteal thickening and/or <u>sclerosis</u>

* Often normal in the first 2–3 weeks of disease onset   [[7]](/library/cy1aVj0)[[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* If the initial <u>radiograph</u> is negative: [[5]](/library/uy1pSj0)

* Suspected <u>low-risk stress fractures</u>: Repeat in 10–14 days.

* Suspected <u>stress</u> <u>fractures</u> of the <u>pelvis</u>, hip, or lower extremity: Obtain early <u>MRI</u>.

* Other suspected <u>high-risk stress fractures</u>: Consider <u>MRI</u>.

* For athletes with any <u>stress</u> <u>fracture</u>: Obtain an <u>MRI</u>.

* <u>MRI</u> without contrast

* High <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u>

* Indications [[4]](/library/by1Hdj0)[[5]](/library/uy1pSj0)

* Early definitive diagnosis required (<u>gold standard</u>)

* Diagnostic uncertainty

* Assessment for return to play required

* Findings include:  [[13]](/library/N4W-jl0)[[14]](/library/akWQml0)

* <u>Fracture</u> line: line of low signal intensity

* <u>Bone marrow</u> and/or periosseous <u>soft tissue</u> <u>edema</u>

* Other imaging modalities: Consider if there is diagnostic uncertainty in patients with <u>contraindications to MRI</u>. [[5]](/library/uy1pSj0)

* <u>Bone scan</u>

* CT

* <u>Ultrasound</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Stress</u> <u>fractures</u> may often not be visible on plain films, particularly during the first 2–3 weeks of disease onset. Repeat <u>x-ray</u> and/or <u>MRI</u> is often required. [[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




![Olecranon stress fracture](media/rqt4k9sryrj5l1qcchimwlfi.jpg)

Olecranon stress fracture

![Edema of the intermediate cuneiform](media/yuirwhg5eiqawvvmj76hb9kt.jpg)

Edema of the intermediate cuneiform




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[15]](/library/FRWgKO0)




* Usually not required

* Consider if there is diagnostic uncertainty or to exclude serious <u>differential diagnoses of stress fractures</u> (e.g., <u>osteomyelitis</u>, <u>malignancy</u>).

* Recommended studies include:

* <u>CMP</u>

* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>ESR</u>

---

## Treatment

Initial <u>management of stress fractures</u> is typically conservative. Surgical management is reserved for refractory cases and <u>high-risk stress fractures</u> (e.g. <u>anterior</u> <u>tibia</u>, <u>proximal</u> 5<sup>th</sup> <u>metatarsal</u>, patella, <u>talus</u>, superolateral femoral neck), which are <u>prone</u> to <u>fracture</u> progression, delayed union, or <u>nonunion</u>.




### <u>Low-risk stress fractures</u> [[10]](/library/zr1rPR0)[[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Cease inciting activity for 4–6 weeks.

* Continue <u>weight-bearing as tolerated</u>.

* Consider splinting or a short <u>walking boot</u> in case of severe symptoms.

* <u>Pain control</u> (e.g., <u>acetaminophen</u>, ice packs)  [[6]](/library/bB1HzQ0)

* <u>Risk factor</u> modification (e.g., improved nutrition, <u>calcium</u> and <u>vitamin D</u> supplementation)

* Screen female patients for <u>female athlete triad</u>. [[2]](/library/Uy1bej0)





> [!TIP]
> Up to one-third of <u>low-risk stress fractures</u> do not heal with <u>conservative management</u>. Refer patients with refractory <u>fractures</u> to orthopedic <u>surgery</u>. [[6]](/library/bB1HzQ0)




### <u>High-risk stress fractures</u> [[2]](/library/Uy1bej0)[[12]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Manage like an acute <u>fracture</u>: See “<u>General principles of fracture management</u>.”

* Immobilize the affected extremity (e.g., cast, <u>splint</u>).

* Advise avoidance of <u>weight-bearing</u> activities.

* <u>Risk factor</u> modification (e.g., improved nutrition, <u>calcium</u> and <u>vitamin D</u> supplementation)

* Refer to orthopedic <u>surgery</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>High-risk stress fractures</u> should be managed like acute <u>fractures</u>. [[2]](/library/Uy1bej0)

---

## Calcaneal stress fractures

<u>Calcaneal stress fractures</u> are most commonly found in individuals who run, jump, and/or march for extended periods of time (e.g., athletes, dancers, soldiers). For acute <u>fractures</u> of the <u>calcaneus</u>, see “<u>Calcaneal fractures</u>.” [[17]](/library/1A12ij0)




### Etiology [[17]](/library/1A12ij0)




* Repetitive microstress to the <u>calcaneus</u> (e.g., weight overload, increase in physical activity)

* Inadequate footwear and activity on hard surfaces increase risk.

* See also “<u>Etiology of stress fractures</u>.”





### Clinical features [[17]](/library/1A12ij0)




* Heel <u>pain</u> on activity (e.g., <u>weight-bearing</u> activities, walking on hard surfaces)

* Point tenderness on palpation of the <u>posterior</u> <u>calcaneus</u>

* Swelling, warmth, and/or <u>ecchymosis</u> of the heel (uncommon)

* Positive calcaneal squeeze test: <u>pain</u> elicited by mediolateral compression of the heel between thumb and index finger





![Calcaneal squeeze test](media/zji4ifiej4xzhy4x6ugqq6eb.jpg)

Calcaneal squeeze test




### Diagnostics




* <u>X-ray</u>: foot series with <u>Harris axial view</u> [[10]](/library/zr1rPR0)

* <u>Fractures</u> may not be visible until 2–3 weeks after onset of clinical features.

* Findings: focal <u>sclerosis</u> in <u>posterior</u> <u>calcaneus</u> (most common)   [[17]](/library/1A12ij0)

* <u>MRI</u>

* Indicated if clinical features and <u>x-rays</u> are equivocal

* Findings: <u>sclerosis</u>, <u>soft tissue</u> changes

* See also “<u>Diagnostics for stress fractures</u>.”





![Calcaneal stress fracture](media/d9ehz4j1d0f3l5ntighj8qy8.jpg)

Calcaneal stress fracture




### Differential diagnosis of chronic heel pain




* <u>Calcaneal stress fracture</u>

* <u>Plantar fasciitis</u>

* <u>Achilles tendinopathy</u>

* <u>Heel pad syndrome</u>

* <u>Tarsal tunnel syndrome</u>

* <u>Calcaneal spur</u> (<u>heel spur</u>)

* <u>Peripheral neuropathy</u>

* <u>Lumbosacral radiculopathy</u>





![Achilles and plantar calcaneal spurs](media/xbpt12u36s7h5067e3tc2m9l.jpg)

Achilles and plantar calcaneal spurs




### Treatment [[17]](/library/1A12ij0)[[18]](/library/PF1WRi0)




<u>Calcaneal stress fractures</u> are considered low-risk and can usually be <u>managed conservatively</u>.




* Activity modification with reduced <u>weight bearing</u>

* Heel pad inserts

* Consider a <u>walking boot</u> and/or <u>shock</u>-absorbing orthotic.

* Routine orthopedic follow up

* See also “<u>Treatment of stress fractures</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> <u>Calcaneal stress fractures</u> are often misdiagnosed as soft-tissue injuries and undertreated. [[17]](/library/1A12ij0)
